item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox are in the playoffs for the second straight year. The clinch became official Sunday when the Braves beat the Astros, guaranteeing Boston a spot in the Wild Card Series starting on September 29.
The roster is not yet complete. Several key arms are still working their way back from injuries, and the next six games at Fenway Park will determine how the pitching staff looks when October arrives.
One of the biggest names on that list took a step forward this week.
Tracy Provides Update on Crochet
Garrett Crochet is closing in on a significant milestone in his comeback. Interim manager Chad Tracy said the plan is for Crochet to throw a live bullpen session against hitters early next week, with Tuesday as the hopeful target.
“Maybe early next week, a potential IBP dependent on how he feels over the next couple days,” Tracy said. “Maybe early next week we’ll be able to face some hitters. But yeah, tentative.”
Crochet’s ramp-up has been deliberate at every stage, and the Red Sox are not going to rush the left-hander into a situation he is not ready for.
Facing live hitters would represent the most significant test of Crochet’s rehab to this point. He threw 30 pitches over two simulated innings earlier this month, and Tracy said at the time that everything went well. A live session against hitters is the next level up.
What Crochet Would Mean for October
Crochet’s potential availability changes the shape of Boston’s postseason pitching plans.
The rotation is lining up with Payton Tolle, Sonny Gray, and Ranger Suarez as the likely starters for the Wild Card Series. Tolle has posted a 2.44 ERA across his last eight starts. Gray has been one of the best starters in the American League this season, carrying a 2.76 ERA.
Adding Crochet would give Tracy another weapon to deploy, albeit from the bullpen.
Tyron Guerrero returned from the injured list Sunday and looked sharp. Aroldis Chapman, Garrett Whitlock, and Erik Miller round out a late-inning group that has carried the pitching staff down the stretch. Tanner Houck continues to progress through minor league rehab and remains a potential option.
Final Word for the Red Sox
Garrett Crochet is not back yet. The live bullpen is tentative. The timeline is still dependent on how his body responds day to day.
The Red Sox have been patient with this process, and that patience could pay off at exactly the right time.
Tuesday will tell the story. If Crochet gets through a live session clean, Boston’s pitching picture for the postseason gets significantly deeper.

The Colorado Rockies are 57–99.
Purple Row After Dark: If the Rockies could steal one player
An absurd rule for absurd times: if the worst team in baseball could steal one player from a playoff club, who should the Rockies take?
One more loss will give them their fourth consecutive 100-loss season, and they are almost certainly going to finish with the worst record in baseball.
These are absurd times for the Rockies, so I have devised an appropriately absurd rule to help them out.
The team with the worst record in baseball gets to steal one player from a playoff team.
There are, naturally, some restrictions. We’re freezing the playoff field as it stood before games on Sunday, September 20. The player has to come from one of those 12 teams, cannot be a pending free agent, and you cannot take the player who leads his team in FanGraphs WAR. The Rockies also inherit the player’s existing contract.
No, one player is not suddenly turning the Rockies into a contender. But could one poached superstar at least keep this thing from becoming five consecutive 100-loss seasons?
Here’s the board:
| Team | Off limits: fWAR leader | Highest available fWAR | Other players worth considering |
| Rays | Junior Caminero (5.2) | Drew Rasmussen (4.7) | Jonathan Aranda (3) |
| Guardians | Parker Messick (4.6) | Steven Kwan (3.4) | Gavin Williams (3.4), Brayan Rocchio (3.3), José Ramírez (2.2) |
| Rangers | Ezequiel Duran (4.6) | Jacob deGrom (4.2) | Josh Jung (2.9), Wyatt Langford (2.8) |
| Yankees | Cam Schlittler (6.1) | Ben Rice (4) | Cody Bellinger (3.9), Aaron Judge (2) |
| Red Sox | Willson Contreras (4.1) | Payton Tolle (4) | Ceddanne Rafaela (3.9), Ranger Suárez (3.7) |
| White Sox | Miguel Vargas (5) | Chase Meidroth (4) | Tristan Peters (3.9), Sean Burke (3.1) |
| Brewers | Jacob Misiorowski (6.3) | Brice Turang (5.4) | Jackson Chourio (4), Jake Bauers (3.6) |
| Dodgers | Shohei Ohtani (6.7) | Yoshinobu Yamamoto (4.7) | Max Muncy (4.3), Andy Pages (3.9) |
| Braves | Chris Sale (5.7) | Michael Harris II (4) | Matt Olson (4), Drake Baldwin (3.1) |
| Cubs | Pete Crow-Armstrong (10.2) | Alex Bregman (5) | Dansby Swanson (3.6) |
| Padres | Fernando Tatis Jr. (5) | Jackson Merrill (4) | Ty France (3.8), Mason Miller (3.7) |
| Phillies | Cristopher Sánchez (5.8) | Jesús Luzardo (5.6) | Zack Wheeler (3.5), Bryce Harper (3.4) |
For me, the choice comes down to Brice Turang, Yoshinobu Yamamoto and Aaron Judge.
Turang is probably the sensible choice.
At 5.4 fWAR, he would easily lead the Rockies, giving them a legitimate top-end player while immediately solving second base for the foreseeable future. He’s 26, hitting .266/.367/.441 with an .808 OPS, and brings value on both sides of the ball with elite range, strong baserunning and a 95th-percentile walk rate.
It would be a very easy way to make the roster better.
But the Rockies really need starting pitching.
Enter Yoshinobu Yamamoto.
He’s 14–8 with a 2.51 ERA, 178 strikeouts and a 0.87 WHIP over 179 innings. His Statcast profile is just as impressive: 100th-percentile pitching run value, 99th-percentile fastball run value, 95th-percentile offspeed run value and a 91st-percentile xERA.
Pitchers are risky, and Yamamoto comes with a lot of money attached. But it’s hard to argue with either the profile or the results, and the addition of the Penner family makes absorbing that contract a lot easier to imagine.
Speaking of high-priced items...
Aaron Judge.
Judge being available is basically a loophole created by our own stupid rule. Injuries have limited him to just 285 plate appearances, which is why he sits at only 2 fWAR, but he’s still hitting .241/.360/.511 with 15 home runs.
And the underlying numbers are still very much Judge: a .396 xwOBA, .569 xSLG, 94.0 mph average exit velocity and a 57.5% hard-hit rate.
It is very hard to look at that and say, “No thanks.”
After all, Aaron Judge is the type of hitter that, if he were playing 81 games a year at Coors Field, I might take out a small loan for season tickets.
So who are you stealing?

Garrett Whitlock is looking to make a career pivot and transition into the starting rotation. For the Boston Red Sox, it's a strange proposition. The right-hander is one of the best setup men in the league, and that has tremendous value.
Of course, starting pitchers have even more value, hence the higher salaries, but the transition is a risk. Not only does a hurler need to reserve something in the tank rather than just air it out for an inning, but he also needs to have enough variation in his arsenal to turn over a lineup multiple times.
Some Red Sox beat writers don't believe the transition is the best idea. The biggest concern is whether or not Whitlock's health can hold up under a starter's workload. The 30-year-old's past forays into starting have resulted in injuries, making this a serious concern and not just some folks crying wolf.
However, there are still reasons to give it a try. Not now, of course. But in 2027, Whitlock in the rotation could make a lot of sense for a few distinct reasons.
The Red Sox should roll the dice on Garrett Whitlock as a starter in 2027
Presumably, the reason Whitlock would like to try his hand again in the rotation is monetary. On the free-agent market, mid-rotation starters can get upwards of $15 million per season. Look at guys like Chris Bassit and Merrill Kelly, for example, who are making $18.5 million and $18 million this season, respectively.
However, Boston holds options for 2027 and 2028 on Whitlock. If exercised, the Red Sox will pay him $8.25 million next year and $10.5 million in 2028. If he works out as a starter, that's an incredible value.
The next reason to give this a go is the fact that Whitlock has the repertoire to work in the rotation. While the majority of relievers are one-or-two-pitch pitchers, Whitlock has three quality offerings. His sinker is the cornerstone, which he throws 56% of the time, but he has a slider and changeup, too.
The slider he uses at a 26% rate, and it generates a ton of whiffs, coming in at 46.7%. The change gets broken out at an 18% clip, is a weapon against lefties, and also has a healthy 35.6% whiff rate. You might like to see a fourth pitch, just to have a show-me offering, but that's a solid foundation for a starter.
The next point is about righty-lefty balance. The Red Sox have an extreme imbalance towards southpaws. Theoretically, if everyone is healthy, you have Garrett Crochet, Ranger Suarez, Payton Tolle, and Jake Bennett all throwing from the left side. If Sonny Gray retires, Boston will have to find a righty to avoid skewing entirely left-handed.
Finally, the risk is minimal. As long as he doesn't suffer a catastrophic injury, the Red Sox can always stick Whitlock back in the bullpen and have a dominant high-leverage reliever should he struggle as a starter. In that regard, they're playing with house money. They control his future for the next two years, and he's paid a reasonable rate for a setup man, and what would be a steal for a No. 3 or No. 4 starter. At that point, why not take the plunge?

ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — The Red Sox will start Payton Tolle, Sonny Gray, and Ranger Suarez in the series against the Guardians that starts Tuesday at Fenway Park.
That would conceivably line them up for the Wild Card Series that starts on Sept. 29 with six days rest each.
“Don’t read into that yet,” interim manager Chad Tracy said Sunday before a 5-1 loss against the Rays. “We can line that up still however we want.”
True. But Tolle has a 2.44 ERA in his last eight starts. He also has faced the Yankees twice this season and allowed one run on four hits over 13 innings with three walks and 18 strikeouts.
Gray allowed three runs on nine hits over 13⅔ innings in two starts against the Yankees. He struck out 12 and walked three.
Guerrero returns
Righthanded reliever Tyron Guerrero returned from a 19-day stint on the injured list with shoulder inflammation. Righthanded reliever Wyatt Olds was optioned to Triple-A Worcester.
Guerrero pitched a perfect eighth inning, striking out two.
“Felt good to be out there,” Guerrero said. “If I get a few more games I’ll be fine [for the postseason].”
Guerrero, 35, was called up in May for his first major league stint since 2019. He emerged as a reliable late-inning option, posting a 3.18 ERA over 39 games.
“He’s obviously a very important piece to this puzzle in our bullpen,” Tracy said.
Olds deserved a better fate. The 27-year-old has a 1.20 ERA and 1.20 WHIP in 13 games since making his major league debut on Aug. 17.
“Very tough. He’s thrown the ball great. He’s got big stuff,” Tracy said. “We had to make a roster decision.”
Contreras doing better
Willson Contreras took some swings in the batting cage to test his bruised right hand and came through fine. He said he hopes to be able to do more on Tuesday. “Step in the right direction,” Tracy said … There was no update on Garrett Crochet, who has yet to face hitters. That could come in the next few days … Tanner Houck had a 3.38 ERA over eight innings in four minor league games. Tracy suggested he would face hitters in a simulated game early this week. “Figuring out the next steps at home — and want to figure that out — but no plans for the next outing,” Tracy said. Could Houck be activated? “It’s possible,” Tracy said. “At this point, it’s going to depend very much on where’s the roster at, what are the needs, and then go from there.”… Rays shortstop Taylor Walls showed his baseball acumen in the first inning. With Roman Anthony on first and one out, he allowed Adley Rutschman’s popup to drop. Walls picked up the ball and flipped to second to get the force on Anthony. That left the Sox with a slower runner on first. It ultimately didn’t matter as Trevor Story struck out … Worcester, as Double-A Portland also did last weekend, had its final game rained out. The WooSox finished 76-67. Kutter Crawford was at Polar Park, and the plan was to have him start what would have been a bullpen game. Crawford has not appeared in a major league game since Sept. 28, 2024. He missed the 2025 season because of an injured right knee. He injured his right wrist in August of that season doing yard work at his home in Florida. Crawford pitched three innings in a rehab game for Worcester on April 11 but had a setback and wasn’t cleared for a game until Sunday. “He got to a point where he wanted to go out there and throw one,” Tracy said.

Boston Red Sox right-hander Kutter Crawford was set to make a rehab start with Triple-A Worcester. But with the game being cancelled due to rain, per the Worcester Telegram-Gazette's Tommy Cassell, the club faces a tough roster decision on the 30-year-old starter.
The cancellation also ends Worcester's season. That means the Red Sox will have to decide if they want to roster Crawford during the final seven games of the regular season, and possibly the postseason.
Crawford is currently on the 60-day injured list after suffering a major setback in his recovery from wrist surgery. After a rehab start in April, he experienced issues in his right elbow and has been shelved since. This appearance would have been his first outing in five months.
Red Sox Face Tough Roster Decision on Kutter Crawford
With nowhere to get a rehab outing, the Red Sox will have to decide the next steps for Kutter Crawford. They certainly had some contingency in place if the game was affected by weather.
The first question the Red Sox have to answer is whether Crawford is an option for the postseason. If not, they will likely just shut him down. Otherwise, they have to clear a 40-man roster spot to activate him from the injured list.
If Boston does roster the 30-year-old, it will likely be in a relief role. The Red Sox will likely go into the Wild Card Series with a three-man rotation of Sonny Gray, Ranger Suarez, and Payton Tolle. If they advance further, they could turn to either Jake Bennett or Brayan Bello as their fourth starter.
Given the postseason in general, there could be some need for an innings-eater for the bullpen. But Bello and Bennett are further stretched out than Crawford at this point in the season.
If Crawford is done for the year, it will mark the second straight season the right-hander has not thrown a pitch for the Red Sox. That could make him a non-tender candidate in November. But if they do tender him, he won't see much of a raise from his $2.75 million salary for 2026.
It's quite possible that Crawford has thrown his last pitch for the Red Sox.
Red Sox Right Now
The Red Sox aim to clinch a postseason berth in their series finale against the Tampa Bay Rays. They'll send left-hander Patrick Sandoval to the mound.
Boston needs a win or a loss by the Houston Astros to officially clinch. They've already been eliminated from American League East contention, so they would be locked into a Wild Card spot.
The Red Sox have a five-game lead for the AL's second Wild Card spot. So they should lock in their postseason seeding in the next couple of days. That would allow them to set up their rotation for the Wild Card Series. Their likely first opponent in the postseason will be the New York Yankees.

item.content:encoded:
They haven’t clinched a postseason berth yet, but it looks more likely by the day that the Boston Red Sox have a date with the New York Yankees in the Wild Card round again.
This will be the third matchup between these two arch rivals in the Wild Card round since 2021, with each organization winning once. The Red Sox got the best of Gerrit Cole in 2021 at Fenway Park, while the Yankees won two straight elimination games to knock off Boston in the Bronx last year.
This series promises to be low-scoring. These two teams are top three in baseball in staff earned run average. The Yankees have nearly three-quarters of a run lead on the Red Sox among starters, while the two bullpens are separated by 0.01 earned runs per nine.
A lot will be made of how these two staffs line up in a couple of weeks. The first two games for the Yankees, as deep as their pitching staff is, seem destined to be Cam Schlittler in Game 1 and Max Fried in Game 2. However, the Red Sox have serious questions to answer about how they want to line up.
Preparing for this series to go the distance is difficult. If you sweep, you line yourselves up well for Game 1 of the American League Division Series. However, if you get swept, one of your best pitchers may never see the hill.
The conundrum is as follows: Sonny Gray has been their best arm wire-to-wire. Payton Tolle is by far their hottest arm, seeming to get stronger as the season wears on. Ranger Suárez is riding two great starts in a row and is their high-priced free agent with elite postseason pedigree.
But of the three, there’s no question who should pitch opposite Schlittler in Game 1: Tolle.
Stats updated prior to games on September 19.
Game 1 Is a Tone-Setter
The dialogue surrounding Game 1 is that it’s almost a “scheduled loss.” To be frank, it’s hard to argue against the logic. In four starts against Boston this year, Schlittler has a 0.74 ERA, a .174 batting average against, and a 27.3% strikeout rate across 24.1 innings.
Let us not forget the sheer domination he exhibited in Game 3 against the Red Sox last year, either. Across eight innings, he allowed five hits, no runs, and struck out 12.
But the mindset for Boston can’t be that it has no chance of winning. Sure, they’ve been one of the league’s best road teams this year, but the Yankees have the best pitching staff in baseball this year for a reason. By comparison, sure, it’s easier to win against someone not in the Cy Young race. But Max Fried habitually finds himself in the discussion for a reason.
The Red Sox’s mindset should be that runs will be at a premium, so matching the Yankees ace zero-for-zero is paramount. Of the three options, Tolle presents the best opportunity to do so. While Gray has Tolle beat overall in ERA, the Red Sox rookie southpaw is, by far, the hottest arm on the staff.
Since the All-Star break, Tolle has a 2.90 ERA with a 28.2% strikeout-to-walk rate. That ERA drops to 2.53 over his last nine starts. That 2.90 ERA, however, is nearly a third of a run better than Gray’s, and over half a run better than Suárez’s.
Sheer run prevention is the name of the game in this series. Tolle is their best option.
Tolle’s Attitude Is Perfect for the Moment
Every time Tolle speaks, he endears himself to the baseball world even more. But as goofy as he can be in media sessions, he’s all business on the field. Furthermore, he can appreciate the moment he’s in at any given time.
Look no further than his recent start against the Kansas City Royals. Eight pitches, eight strikes, six whiffs, all fastballs. He had the wherewithal to glance at pitching coach Andrew Bailey, grin, lock back in and pick up the final strike of an immaculate inning.
Sure, it’s one pitch in the first inning against a team out of postseason contention, but talk to anybody who’s played, and they’ll tell you how aware they are of when they’re on the brink of something cool. Tolle said as much after the game.
But that moment should tell the world he’s unafraid of going into the Bronx, facing off against Schlittler, and going band-for-band with the likely AL Cy Young.
Tolle clearly cares about what he does, but it’s that somewhat unserious attitude that makes him perfect for the high stakes of setting the tone in a postseason series.
This moment, honestly, seemed set in stone the moment he made his MLB debut last season against Paul Skenes. While any postseason start is high leverage, he’s always finding himself making big starts against the game’s best. He’s always met the moment, and the Red Sox should let him continue that trend this postseason.
The Yankees Struggle Against Hard Fastballs
The Yankees are a deep, talented team even if not all players are at full strength or potential going into October. One area where they struggle, however, is against hard fastballs.
This season, the Yankees have the highest strikeout rate on fastballs 95 mph or harder, to go with the second-worst expected batting average. Only the Chicago White Sox are worse against such fastballs.
They’re even worse this season on hard fastballs thrown by left-handers. Their 33% strikeout rate is the second-highest behind the 61-93 Athletics, while their .191 expected batting average ranks only higher than the Cleveland Guardians.
Tolle isn’t positioned with an elite-level fastball from a velocity standpoint, but it’s comfortably above average. This season, he’s in the 71st percentile with an average fastball of 95.7 mph. Opponents struggle mightily against it as well, hitting just .190 with a .248 expected wOBA and a 30.4% whiff rate.
Tolle throws his four-seam and sinker a combined 68.4% of the time. While that leaves him susceptible to predictability, he varies that look with a cutter that comes in at 88.6 mph on average. He throws that offering at a 19.4% clip.
His strength is his fastball, along with 98th percentile extension. That plays directly into the weaknesses of the Yankees lineup. With Game 1 very much being a tone-setter, there’s no question who the Red Sox should send out there.
Lining It Up After Tolle
Following Tolle, the Red Sox have their two veterans waiting in the wings. Win Game 1, you’ve got two proven performers to help you win one more game to advance. Lose Game 1, you’ve got two experienced professionals tasked with staving off elimination.
The order after Tolle almost doesn’t matter. Could they vary looks and go to Gray to keep the Yankees off the lefty scent? Maybe, but then you potentially run into the same problem of playing with your food. That said, Suárez is much craftier than Tolle, and prone to the hanging breaking ball.
The Yankees have a 99 wRC+ as a team against right-handed pitching, and a 107 against lefties. Gray also took a no-hitter into the eighth inning against the Yankees back in late June, while Suárez was touched up in his last start against them.
What can be said either way is that having two accomplished veterans to follow the rookie gunslinger is a good position for the Red Sox to be in.

ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. - There was no celebration, but there was a revelation.
The Red Sox couldn't close the deal in securing a postseason berth, succumbing to a Rays 2-1 walk-off win at Tropicana Field on Saturday. But an interesting development emerged along the way. Brayan Bello is suddenly a potential huge part of the postseason solution.
The almost out-of-nowhere conversation about Bello's importance was given an enormous boost by one of the pitcher's best outings of his career. Not only did Bello hold the Rays to just one run over eight innings, but he also struck out 11 and walked no one.
Why was this even more impressive than simply the end-of-day box score? Because Bello managed all those punchouts, along with 17 whiffs, against a Rays team that has struck out fewer times than any club in baseball. No starting pitcher had managed double-digit strikeouts against Tampa Bay, with Toronto's Dylan Cease coming the closest with nine.
Bello matches his career high with 11 strikeouts! pic.twitter.com/NA2a2pDcAy
— Red Sox (@RedSox) September 19, 2026
The dominance was just what the doctor ordered for Bello and the Red Sox, even if starting a postseason game isn't in the righty's immediate future.
While there has been no announcement, it appears the Red Sox are lining up their wild-card rotation with Payton Tolle to pitch Game 1 against the Yankees, followed by Sonny Gray and then Ranger Suarez if Game 3 is needed in the best-of-three series. But that doesn't mean Bello can't have an impact on outcomes from late September into October.
Bello's fastball routinely sat at 97 mph, almost two mph above his season-average velocity. It was a fastball that got nine whiffs, with the Rays coming away with just four hard-hit balls all day.
"That was exceptional," Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy said. "By far and away, his best outing of the year, as good as I've seen him, so, I don't know what else to say, he was awesome. Really awesome."
Bello's appearance allowed for thoughts on what might be in store for his effectiveness out of the bullpen in high-leverage situations come Sept. 29. It has been well-documented what he can do as a reliever, posting a 1.98 ERA in 15 games out of the bullpen this season. But now we're not just talking about bulk roles or giving the Red Sox some length.
This version of Bello can absolutely be a late-inning, high-leverage weapon.
For instance, while we aren't sure of Aaron Judge's health heading into the postseason, if the Yankees' slugger does play, this might not be a bad reminder to put in your statistical back pocket: Judge is just 2-for-21 with eight strikeouts against Bello.
While some naysayers might point to the less-than-inspiring appearances Bello has turned in at Yankee Stadium as of late, including maybe his worst relief outing of the season at the end of August when he allowed four runs over 4 1/3 innings, or the 2 1/3-inning start in Game 2 of last season's wild card round. But before those two, the pitcher had been absolutely nails in the Bronx, totaling a 1.44 ERA in five starts.
Assuming their health is OK, the Red Sox will have Aroldis Chapman and Garrett Whitlock at the ready to help close out games. But with a week to go in the regular season, there is some uncertainty regarding the late-inning options. Saturday, Bello sure seemed like he was ready to help with that.
“For me, it's just showing the team that I'm ready for these kind of games,” Bello said. “Also, them giving me the opportunity to pitch today was a good step for that. And I thank them for giving me the confidence and the opportunity to start again.”

item.content:encoded:
Can you believe the playoffs are almost here? A week from today the Red Sox will wrap up their regular season, closing the book on what has been among the most unexpected, topsy turvy seasons we’ve ever seen. From there the playoffs await, and who knows what twists and turns may still be in store.
But before we get there, what business is there left for the Red Sox to get squared away before Game 1 of the Wild Card series? We answer your questions in today’s Red Sox mailbag.
Tanner Houck and Garrett Crochet both appear close to ready to return. What is the chance that the Red Sox decide to put both of them on the postseason roster? Each feels like a high upside question mark but is it too risky relying on both of them to excel in limited roles? — Paul from Bluesky
If the Red Sox decide they’re ready I think there’s a great chance both pitch in the playoffs. The question of whether or not it’s too risky is valid, but the other factor to consider is would it be riskier to let an inferior arm take the mound at Yankee Stadium with the season on the line.
The nature of a best-of-three playoff series compared to a best-of-five or even a best-of-seven also makes the idea of loading up on short-inning relievers more attractive.
The Red Sox will only need three starting pitchers in the first round, presumably Sonny Gray, Ranger Suarez and Payton Tolle, in some order. That effectively frees up two additional bullpen spots, one of which I’m guessing will be filled by Jake Bennett as an emergency bulk man should the starter exit early due to injury or poor performance.
The back end of the bullpen is pretty much set in stone. If everyone is healthy and available it will be Aroldis Chapman, Garrett Whitlock, Erik Miller and Tyron Guerrero locking down the high leverage innings. But after that the Red Sox have some interesting decisions to make.
In one group you have the other short men, including Greg Weissert, Jovani Moran and Wyatt Olds. Then in the next group you have the longer men, including Patrick Sandoval, Brayan Bello, Alec Gamboa and Raymond Burgos. Finally, you have Crochet, Houck and Johan Oviedo, who has also begun a rehab assignment after missing nearly the entire season. What the Red Sox have to decide is which five of those 10 options give you the best chance to win?
I don’t think you can dispute that Crochet and Houck have the highest ceiling of that bunch, so if they’re good to go I don’t think the Red Sox will hesitate to give them the nod.
With Romy Gonzalez now hitting so well in Worcester, do you see him being put on the postseason roster as a lefty masher, and one of Isiah Kiner-Falefa, Andruw Monasterio or Jahmai Jones being left off? — @wcbosox on Bluesky
If the Red Sox believe Romy Gonzalez gives them the best chance to win in October, I feel like it would make sense for them to call him up and get him some looks at big league pitching over the last two weeks. You could make a great case that they should — he was batting .360 in 23 games since being optioned to Triple-A entering Friday — but if that doesn’t happen then that could be a sign the Red Sox don’t see him as part of the October plan.
Either way, the club has some tough decisions to make as far as constructing the bench goes.
Presuming that Ceddanne Rafaela returns from the IL without any issues and Willson Contreras isn’t sidelined by his hand injury, the Red Sox should enter the playoffs with a starting lineup featuring Adley Rutschman at catcher, Contreras, Nick Sogard, Trevor Story and Caleb Durbin across the infield, and an outfield of Rafaela, Wilyer Abreu, Roman Anthony and Jarren Duran, with one of Anthony or Duran presumably starting at designated hitter if a righty is on the mound.
That leaves four spots for Kiner-Falefa, Monasterio, Jones, Mickey Gasper, Connor Wong, Nate Eaton, Gonzalez and possibly Curtis Mead. For our purposes we can probably set aside Eaton, who will likely be optioned upon Rafaela’s activation, as well as Mead, who only just started swinging a light bat and won’t have the benefit of a rehab assignment prior to his return.
Let’s also set aside some of the more outside the box candidates like Braiden Ward, who has never appeared in a big league game but who may garner consideration as a late-inning pinch runner after stealing 60 bases at Triple-A.
One spot will go to a backup catcher, and while you could talk yourself into Gasper filling that role, Wong has the most familiarity with the pitching staff and the Red Sox would probably rather keep Gasper available as a pinch hitter without worrying about catching logistics.
How about the other three spots? Kiner-Falefa, Monasterio and Gonzalez are all versatile infield defenders who bat right-handed, so there’s some redundancy there. Jones also bats right-handed and could function as an emergency reserve outfielder in addition to his pinch hitter, and while Gasper is technically a switch hitter, his real value comes from the left side, where he’s crushed righties over the past month.
What’s going to happen? My guess is the bench will be Wong, Gasper, Jones and one of the three righty infielders. So to go back to your original question, could Gonzalez make the playoff roster over one of Kiner-Falefa, Monasterio or Jones? Yes, and in fact even if he doesn’t make the roster one of those guys could still wind up on the outside looking in.
If the playoffs started today who would be the starting second baseman? Also, what’s the long-term plan for that position? — Tom P.
If the playoffs started today I think Nick Sogard would be the clear choice to start at second base. He’s been an everyday player for the Red Sox since the end of July, and at a time where most of the offense has hit a skid Sogard has been a reliable contributor at the plate, batting .262 with five home runs and a .772 OPS entering the weekend since being called back up on July 29.
Long-term, the Red Sox have a couple of different candidates who could emerge in the coming years.
If he hadn’t broken his wrist in his team debut I think it’s safe to say Curtis Mead would have spent the past two months starting at second for the Red Sox. Prior to the trade he was in the midst of a breakout season with the Washington Nationals, and at only 25 years old there’s good reason to believe his best years are still ahead of him. Whether he returns in the playoffs or for the start of next season, Mead should have the best chance to claim second base for himself.
But outside of him, Sogard and perhaps Gonzalez or Anthony Seigler, there is one other wild card. That’s Franklin Arias.
The top Red Sox prospect is putting the finishing touches on a brilliant season, and if he continues to develop he should have a great chance of becoming a key building block, perhaps as soon as next year. With Story under contract for only one more season he will have an opportunity to slide right into the starting shortstop job entering 2028, but what if he proves he’s ready for primetime before that? In that case Arias might get an initial look at second, with Mead perhaps rotating between the designated hitter spot and occasionally giving Durbin and Contreras a breather at their corner infield positions.
Does MLB need to readjust its postseason schedule? The No. 2 or 3 team in the American League will be eliminated in a three-game series, meanwhile two teams that are barely .500 play each other in the first round. — Brandon C.
I like the idea that there should be a reward for winning your division. If you’re one of the top two division winners you get a first round bye, and if you’re the third division winner you at least get to host the best-of-three Wild Card series. I’m fine with that, even in a weird year like this where all of the American League’s best teams are in the same division and the other division leaders are mediocre at best.
But the problem is what happens afterwards. Like you said, the No. 2 and 3 teams in the AL are probably going to wind up being the Yankees and Red Sox, and whichever of those teams advances will have to play the No. 1 seeded Tampa Bay Rays. Meanwhile, all three teams on the other side of the bracket could potentially finish with worse records than anyone on the AL East side, and one of those clubs will be guaranteed a trip to the ALCS.
I think MLB could address this by reseeding after the Wild Card round. The top two division winners would still get home field advantage in their divisional series, but whichever team advancing out of the Wild Card round has the better record would be paired with the second division winner. So this year if the Red Sox beat the Yankees and let’s say the AL West champion wins their Wild Card series, the Red Sox would go on to play the AL Central champion instead of the Rays, while the AL West champion would get Tampa Bay even though they would have technically started the playoffs as the higher seed.
Most years it probably won’t make a huge difference, but reseeding ahead of the divisional round would strike a balance between preserving the incentives for winning your division while ensuring the bracket doesn’t become unbalanced.

item.content:encoded:
There were many questions the New York Yankees needed Spencer Jones to answer this season. Now, we've seen enough of him, even if it's been in a couple of disjointed stints, to get a good idea of who he is at the major league level.
The answer: pretty damn good. After struggling early, Jones has found his footing. A big reason for his ascendancy has been surprising. The Vanderbilt product has mashed left-handed pitching.
He's now logged 51 plate appearances against lefties and has slashed an eye-watering .435/.490/.761 following his homer off Minnesota Twins lefty specialist Taylor Rodgers on Sept. 15. It was the first dinger Rodgers gave up to a left-handed hitter over 133 plate appearances this season.
The sample size isn't huge, but it's relatively significant. For example, Ben Rice has 209 plate appearances against lefties out of his 622 plate appearances. For Jones, the 51 matchups against southpaws are a decent portion of his 255 total plate appearances.
One of the most impressive things about how he's performed against same-handed pitching is the amount of power he's demonstrated. Obviously, the six-foot-seven outfielder is a behemoth, but most lefties, even those who perform well against southpaws, see a drop in power in those situations. Take Rice, for instance; his slugging percentage drops from .561 against righties to .457 against left-handers. That hasn't been the case for Jones.
This has just been one part of Jones' maturation process that should have every fan feeling confident about not only his future, but his ability to contribute now.
Spencer Jones' performance against lefties has Yankees well-positioned for playoffs vs. Red Sox
Overall, Jones is hitting .259/.331/.452 with 10 homers on the season. He's been even better since being recalled on July 22, posting a .271/.337/.490 line with eight of his 10 homers coming during this most recent span.
There should be no more doubt that he should start over Trent Grisham, assuming Grisham is healthy, once the playoffs roll around. A significant part of that reasoning has to do with his performance against southpaws.
Jones has learned a lot from Cody Bellinger on how to handle those tough at-bats since he's been up in the bigs and the star left fielder has been healthy.
“When we are in the dugout, he’s one of those people I can go up to and ask, like, ‘Yo, what did you see?’ He’ll tell me bluntly what he saw, how he saw it, and essentially what he’s going to do next time. It’s like, all right, good to know before I go even into my first (at-bat) what this MVP is going to do for his first at-bat. It’s pretty sweet knowing that I’ve got these guys to help me out,” Jones said to The Athletic this week.
He couldn't have a better mentor. Bellinger isn't hitting lefties as much as he did last year, when he put up an insane .353/.415/.601 line, but his .287/.346/.449 performance in 2026 is plenty good, and better than what he's done against righties. In fact, Bellinger is about as balanced as they come with an .804 career OPS against left-handers and an .819 mark against righties.
We spoke about Rice earlier, but the early-season drama about his usage against lefties is a thing of the past. While he has more pop against righties, Rice's .255/.330/.457 line against southpaws is more than serviceable.
Despite having so many lefties in the lineup on a daily basis, the Yankees as a whole don't suffer much from it. The club is hitting a collective .247/.318/.422 against left-handed pitching this season, with a .740 OPS that ranks ninth. Remember, for most of that time, Aaron Judge hasn't been a factor, either.
Looking ahead, the Yankees' most likely opponent in the Wild Card series is the Red Sox, who are loaded with left-handers. In the rotation, they boast southpaws Payton Tolle and Ranger Suárez, with their being a possibility that Jake Bennett makes the cut, too. In the bullpen, they'll hope to unleash Garrett Crochet, Erik Miller and old friend Aroldis Chapman.
However, rather than being overmatched, we might say that this plays into the Yankees' hands. New York can handle left-handed pitching, and those lefty bats can tee off against righties. Jones emerging as a threat against southpaws only solidifies the strength and gives the Yankees another regular who doesn't need a platoon partner, allowing them to match up only where they're vulnerable.

We're just over one week away from the 2026 Major League Baseball regular season coming to a close. Then, the entire focus around the league will turn to the playoffs. When it comes to the Boston Red Sox, they will be in the mix.
The Red Sox haven't officially clinched yet, although that could happen as soon as Saturday. As the playoffs have inched closer and closer, one topic that has lingered around Boston is the starting rotation. The rotation is loaded and it's a real question of how the club will sort it out ahead of a Wild Card round series, very likely against the New York Yankees. Sonny Gray has seemed like the likely choice, but that may not be the case.
Could Boston Turn To The Rookie?
Do you roll with the veteran in Game 1? He has been among the best pitchers in the league in general all season to this point. Ranger Suárez has been red-hot recently and was brought to town because of the fact that he has been electric in the playoffs throughout his career to this point. Also, of course, there's Payton Tolle, who is also red-hot right now. On Saturday, Rob Bradford of WEEI shared on X that Tolle actually has a "good shot" at nabbing the Game 1 spot.
"It sure looking like Tolle has a good shot at pitching Game 1 the way they are lining things up," Bradford wrote on X.
Gray has been among the best pitchers in baseball this season. He has a 2.82 ERA and a 146-to-45 strikeout-to-walk ratio in 163 innings pitched this season. Gray also is leading the league with 17 wins. He has been Boston's ace all season. Since Aug. 15, Gray has a 2.89 ERA and a 3-2 record. Since Sep. 4, Suárez has a 0.92 ERA and a 3-0 record. Since Aug. 13, Tolle has a 2.50 ERA and a 42-to-9 strikeout-to-walk ratio in 36 innings pitched across six starts.
Frankly, Boston would be in a good position with any of these three starting Game 1. But in a three-game series, there are even more reasons to get the decision right.
Tolle has made two starts against New York this season and has allowed one run in 13 innings pitched (0.69 ERA) with 18 strikeouts. Gray has made two starts against New York and has allowed three runs in 13 2/3 innings pitched (1.98 ERA) with 12 strikeouts.
Suárez has made three starts against New York and has allowed 11 runs in 16 1/3 innings pitched (5.94 ERA. Of the three, Tolle has fared the best against New York, so the fact that he has a "good shot" at starting Game 1 actually makes a lot of sense.
All three of these guys are red-hot at the moment. Slotting in Tolle for a Game 1, the righty Gray for a Game 2 and then back to a lefty in Suárez for Game 3 — if necessary — arguably is the best bet for a New York series.

Sonny Gray? Ranger Suarez? Payton Tolle? Who should get the ball in game one in the Bronx for the Red Sox?
To manage the starting rotation workload and line up the rotation for the playoffs, the Boston Red Sox are turning to Brayan Bello to start Saturday's game against the Tampa Bay Rays. Whether the Red Sox go with Sonny Gray, Ranger Suarez, or Payton Tolle, the team will feel very good about its chances of winning. However, if the team gets swept, it risks leaving an incredible arm on the bench.
Let's take a look at the argument for each of the trio to get the ball in game one:
Gray
The 36-year-old veteran has inarguably been the Red Sox' best starter in 2026. After entering the season with questions about how effective he could be late in his career, Gray has passed every test with flying colors. In 28 starts, Gray has posted a 2.82 ERA, the eighth-lowest mark in the league, while the Red Sox have gone 20-8 on his start days.
Most importantly, even when he doesn't have his best stuff, he has done well to limit damage; of his 28 starts, he has allowed more than three runs on four occasions. In two starts against the New York Yankees in 2026, Gray has allowed only three earned runs on nine hits, while striking out 12 and walking only four. In his career, Gray has a solid record of playoff success, posting a 3.26 ERA in 30.1 innings.
However, when it comes to elite strikeout stuff that can completely shut down a lineup, Gray lacks that, posting a rather pedestrian strikeouts per nine innings of 8.06, which ranks 30th out of 48 qualified starters.
Still though, Gray appears to be the most obvious choice to get the start in game one.
Suarez
The Red Sox' most difficult decision with their postseason rotation may be the one they have to make with Suarez. The 30-year-old All-Star signed a five-year, $130-million deal with the Red Sox in the offseason, in part because he posted an impressive 1.48 ERA over 42.2 innings with the Philadelphia Phillies.
However, of the trio in consideration, Suarez has been the shakiest since the All-Star break, posting a 3.46 ERA in his last 10 starts. However, the three-time All-Star has been better lately, allowing only two earned runs in 19.2 innings across three starts. Suarez has struggled against the Yankees in three starts in 2026, allowing 11 runs on 20 hits for a 6.06 ERA.
Still, it seems unlikely the team would risk leaving its $130 million investment on the sidelines for a playoff series.
Tolle
The 23-year-old rookie has been Boston's best starter since the All-Star break. In his last 10 starts, Tolle has posted a 2.90 ERA while striking out 12.05 batters per nine innings, the fifth-highest mark among 93 pitchers with at least 50 innings pitched.
Tolle has also performed incredibly well against the Yankees, allowing only one earned run on four hits while striking out 18 and walking only four. Tolle is also the only pitcher on the Boston staff with the electric stuff that could match New York ace Cam Schlittler in shutting down the lineup.
While it certainly may seem risky to some to give a 23-year-old rookie the ball in game one in Yankee Stadium, how can you risk not throwing him at all?
Up next for the Sox
With their magic number down to two, the Red Sox will look to win a series against the likely American League East champion Tampa Bay Rays on Saturday afternoon. Brayan Bello (6-7, 4.74 ERA) will get the start for Boston opposite Freddy Peralta (9-11, 4.67 ERA) will start for Tampa. First pitch from Tropicana Field is set for 4:10 p.m. ET.

ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — When Roman Anthony returned to the Boston Red Sox three weeks ago after nearly four months on the injury list with a torn right finger ligament, it initially looked as if he had barely missed any time.
Through his first five games after he was activated Aug. 30 in New York, Anthony recorded four games with multiple hits, going 10-for-22 with two homers, two doubles and a triple. His methodical rehab, missing 101 games, paid dividends with a bat that was ready to perform.
Advertisement
But then, as so often happens in baseball, he fell out of rhythm at the plate, collecting just seven hits, including just one extra-base hit, in his next 56 plate appearances.
That’s why he found himself in an early batting practice session Friday afternoon with hitting coach John Soteropulos, tinkering in the cage with a few mechanical adjustments.
The work clicked.
Oh baby, Roman! pic.twitter.com/aP7bBEgZX0
— Red Sox (@RedSox) September 18, 2026
Three pitches into the game, Anthony clubbed a solo homer for a lead, and in the second inning, he smacked a bases-loaded single to drive in two more runs as the Red Sox beat the Tampa Bay Rays 4-2, snapping the Rays’ six-game win streak. The win inched the Red Sox closer to clinching a playoff berth. A Red Sox win Saturday, coupled with a Texas Rangers loss, would punch Boston’s ticket to the playoffs.
“We came out and looked really good offensively in the first part of that game, and there was a lot of energy in the dugout,” interim manager Chad Tracy said. “I think guys feel it. We’re not done yet, but I definitely think they sniff it, and we’re wanting to get there for sure.”
With eight games left in the regular season, getting Anthony’s bat hot again, particularly as Willson Contreras remains day to day with a deeply bruised right hand, will be imperative for the Red Sox lineup in the postseason.
“He will,” Tracy said confidently about Anthony’s bat regaining momentum. “I mean, you see what he can do. It’s the game of baseball, there’s ebbs and flows. He came off the rehab, and for like five games, he looked fantastic. Then he went through some stuff, and now he’s starting to look good again. When he’s going well, you see the impact he can make.”
Before Soteropulos was elevated to lead hitting coach this season after an overhaul of the coaching staff, he was the minor-league hitting coordinator and worked closely with Anthony. That relationship has helped.

“Me and John have been working on some things, really since I have been back,” Anthony said. “He’s amazing. He’s somebody who knows my swing so well. We have been together since I came into this org, all throughout the minor leagues. Having somebody here, somebody who knows my swing and when to talk and when to tinker. Nobody knows me better than John.
“It’s such a constant game of adjustments and looking over a span of my last few at-bats, it obviously was not where I wanted to be. I was hitting the ball on the ground, to the right side, so I was trying to get away from that. Hitting early on the field with John and with Trevor (Story) definitely helped.”
Anthony’s first-inning homer came off the bat at an estimated 107.7 mph with an estimated distance of 438 feet, marking the longest homer of his career.
But to him, the two-run single was just as important. In a rough series in Texas, the Red Sox had gone just 1-for-18 with runners in scoring position. His goal was to alleviate some pressure on the offense by simply making contact.
“That’s my job, to do everything I can to put the ball in play and find ways on base,” he said. “That’s how I have had a lot of success in the past as a leadoff hitter. So over these last games, just keep putting an emphasis on being the best leadoff hitter I can be. See as many pitches I can and try and get on base. It was a huge way to start the game. This game is all about momentum, so any time you can get something like that going, it’s huge.”
The two-run single gave the Red Sox the lead back after the Rays tied the score off Ranger Suarez in the bottom of the first. Jahmai Jones made it 4-1 in the third with his sixth homer of the year.
The insurance gave the Red Sox a cushion as Suarez was uncharacteristically spotty with command, walking a career-high five batters.

Still, he navigated traffic in each of the first four innings and allowed just the one run on three hits in 5 2/3 innings. Reliever Wyatt Olds wiggled out of a jam in the sixth after Suarez exited, walking two batters to load the bases, then falling behind pinch hitter Jake Fraley 3-1. Olds came back to strike out Fraley.
The Red Sox faced more trouble in the ninth, with reliever Erik Miller still searching for his command. Closer Aroldis Chapman remains day to day with lat tightness, and Tracy turned to Miller for the ninth with Garrett Whitlock having a heavy load of late.
Miller allowed a run in the ninth on an infield single, a wild pitch, a walk and a groundout. He loaded the bases after a strikeout got away on a wild pitch, but escaped the jam with a groundout to close it out.
Clinching their postseason spot with a week left in the regular season would allow the Red Sox to breathe and reset some players before the postseason. But they’re not there yet. Saturday awaits.
“It just kind of felt like a playoff game,” Anthony said. “Getting into that mode is huge from an at-bat standpoint and from a big-game standpoint of constantly being the next man up.”

ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — A year ago, as the Red Sox crept toward the end of the regular season, the pitching choices for their looming Wild Card Series in New York were limited. Beyond ace Garrett Crochet, who dominated the Yankees in Game 1, the Red Sox ended up going with the unreliable Brayan Bello in Game 2 and the untested Connelly Early in Game 3. Two losses later, they were packing their bags for the winter.
This year, with a replay of that series feeling all but certain to begin a week from Tuesday and once again in the Bronx, the pitching plans look nothing like they did back then.
Which is good news for the Red Sox.
Even with Crochet sidelined all season by injury, the pitching rotation has been, in the words of interim manager Chad Tracy, “pivotal” to the drastic midseason turnaround that lifted this team from the depths of the American League standings and into the playoff race.
A trade for Sonny Gray. The continued development of Payton Tolle. And the free agent signing of Ranger Suarez. Three big moves, three likely starters for one more entry in the ongoing Boston/New York postseason clash of baseball titans.
Friday night in Florida, it was Suarez’s turn to prove his readiness. Facing the first-place Rays presented an obvious test, but for Suarez, it also was a chance to build on his two previous starts, in which he allowed only one run in 14 innings. As Tracy pointed out before the game, there is no mystery into what makes a good Suarez outing. Control the tempo, get ahead in the count, and locate pitches. When the lefthander does those three things, he can be pretty hard to beat.
But, as the Rays learned Friday, even if he doesn’t quite do those three things as well as he wants to, he can still find a way to battle through.
So there he was at the end of a decidedly mixed bag of a night, leading the Sox to a 4-2 win, improving his record to 8-4 after giving up just one run in 5⅔ innings. On the upside, he struck out five and consistently got key outs in key moments.
On the downside, he had to labor mightily to get there, walking a career-high five batters, throwing just 56 of his 98 pitches for strikes. He got away with it this time, but come the playoffs, that’s playing with fire, whether against the Yankees or perhaps the Rays again, with Tampa Bay in line to host the wild-card winners.
The Sox chose to take the positive out of the night.
“When I issued those walks, I think that the game was taking me to a place that wasn’t the right one. So I just tried to take a deep breath and slow it down, and I was able to then take it from there,” Suarez said.
He struck out Yandy Díaz to end the second inning, stranding two runners on base. He got out of another jam in the third, a Chandler Simpson hard-hit line out to right and a strikeout of Jonny DeLuca to strand two more runners.
Suarez did it again in the fourth, helping his own cause by starting a nifty inning-ending double play, snaring Taylor Walls’s line drive to the mound and then throwing to first to double off Nick Fortes.
A clean fifth ended on a called third strike to Junior Caminero, but gave way to a messier sixth, with a leadoff walk to Ryan Vilade eventually leading Tracy to pull the plug as Suarez approached 100 pitches. But not before he struck out DeLuca to get the first out.
“He’s a very good competitor and a really good pitcher,” Tracy said, “that even when he’s got traffic, you trust that he’s going to find his way through it. . . . He walked five, but still almost completed six innings. He was very competitive with men on base.”
“I got traffic every single inning because of the walks, but I was able to limit damage today, and that was part of it,” Suarez said. “It was one of those nights that you didn’t have the command, but I was able to turn the page quickly and was able to get outs when I needed.”
Good as the escape act was, it’s all just staging for what comes next, a playoff berth the Red Sox could clinch on Saturday. Suarez was signed in part because of his experience in the postseason, earned across eight seasons with the Phillies. Suarez is 4-1 with a 1.48 ERA in 11 playoff appearances, which includes eight starts. He was the winner of Game 3 of the 2022 World Series, beating the eventual champion Astros with five shutout innings.
The Phillies also called on him to come out of the bullpen in Game 5 of the NLCS, and all he did was earn his first postseason save by getting two outs on two pitches, stranding the winning run and clinching the Series berth.
“When you get to this part of the season, not every outing is going to go perfectly. But he’s been there and done that as far as navigating his way through an outing and finding a way to strand base runners,” Tracy said. “The game’s not going to speed up on him. You know, even if he’s walked some and there’s some people on base, he doesn’t ever look like he speeds up. He just keeps making his pitches.”

Roman Anthony Powers Red Sox Past Rays, Closer To Playoff Berth originally appeared on NESN. Add NESN as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
The Boston Red Sox spent much of Friday night walking a tightrope. Roman Anthony made sure they had enough of a cushion to survive. Anthony homered and drove in three runs, Ranger Suárez battled through 5 2/3 innings and the Red Sox held on for a 4-2 victory over the Tampa Bay Rays at Tropicana Field.
Boston improved to 84-70 with its second consecutive victory and snapped Tampa Bay's six-game winning streak. The Red Sox entered the series opener with a magic number of three to clinch an American League wild-card berth and could secure their postseason spot as early as Saturday.
It was not a comfortable victory.
Red Sox pitchers issued nine walks, including four over the final four innings. The Rays loaded the bases in both the sixth and ninth but went 0-for-13 with runners in scoring position and stranded 12 runners. Erik Miller finally ended the ninth-inning adventure by getting Chandler Simpson to ground out with the bases loaded.
Here are three takeaways from Boston's important victory.
Roman Anthony Sets Tone Immediately
Anthony did not wait long to make his presence felt. The Red Sox rookie crushed Ian Seymour's third pitch of the game 438 feet to center field, giving Boston a 1-0 lead before most of the announced crowd of 23,342 had settled into its seats.
It was Anthony's fifth home run of the season and the third leadoff homer of his young career. The Rays answered in the bottom of the first when Junior Caminero drove in Yandy Díaz with a groundout, but Anthony struck again one inning later.
Trevor Story singled and Caleb Durbin followed with another base hit. After Nate Eaton walked to load the bases, Anthony delivered a two-out single to right that scored Story and Durbin. Anthony finished 2-for-5 with three RBIs, accounting for nearly all of Boston's offense on one of the biggest nights of its season.
Jahmai Jones supplied the other run by launching a 414-foot solo homer to left in the third inning. Jones' sixth home run gave Boston a 4-1 advantage that held until the ninth.
Ranger Suárez Bends Without Breaking
Suárez rarely had a clean inning, but the left-hander consistently found his way out of trouble. The Boston starter allowed only three hits and one run while striking out five. He also issued five walks and needed 98 pitches to record 17 outs.
His best defensive moment came in the fourth inning.
Taylor Walls hit a 100-mph line drive directly back at Suárez, who made the catch before throwing to first base to double off Nick Fortes. The play erased a scoring opportunity and helped Suárez navigate another stressful inning. The left-hander improved to 8-4 and lowered his ERA to 3.27.
Wyatt Olds entered with two outs in the sixth and immediately made matters worse by issuing two walks. He recovered to strike out Jake Fraley with the bases loaded, preserving Boston's three-run advantage.
Greg Weissert provided the calmest portion of the night, allowing one hit over two scoreless innings.
Erik Miller Survives Chaotic Ninth Inning
The Red Sox carried a 4-1 lead into the ninth, but Miller turned the final three outs into a full-blown ordeal. The left-hander issued two walks and threw three wild pitches during a 32-pitch inning. Jonathan Aranda drove in one run with a fielder's choice, cutting Boston's lead to 4-2.
Tampa Bay eventually loaded the bases with two outs, bringing Simpson to the plate as the potential winning run. Miller induced a ground ball to third baseman Durbin, who completed the force play at second to end the game. Miller earned his fifth save despite allowing one run, one hit and two walks.
Boston will take the victory, especially at this stage of the season, but the nine walks gave the club another issue to clean up before October. The Red Sox will attempt to clinch their postseason berth Saturday when they continue the three-game series in Tampa Bay. The Rays are scheduled to start right-hander Freddy Peralta, while Boston has yet to announce it's starter.

ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — It was by no means a textbook display of pitching. There were walks in each of the first four innings, and a career-high five in all.
There were deep counts, lots of traffic and 98 pitches required in fewer than six innings.
But what counts most is not the strikes or the 1-2-3 innings, but the final score. So a taut 4-2 victory for the Red Sox over the Tampa Bay Rays was, especially at this time of year, reward enough.
"I think it was OK," shrugged Suarez afterward. "I had traffic every single inning because of the walks, but I was able to limit damage today and that was part of it."
Suarez had difficulty explaining how the walks piled up on him. It wasn't mechanical, and it wasn't the result of nibbling around the strike zone.
"I think it was one of those nights when I didn't have the command," he said. "But I was able to get outs when I needed."
The latter has always been his calling card. In an era when most starters unleash fastballs at 95 mph or better, Suarez thrives by mixing pitches, keeping hitters off balance and inducing soft contact.
On nights when he can't locate with precision, the margin for error slips further. But again, knowing how to get out of trouble is a mound skill in and of itself.
Suarez has used that talent particularly well in the postseason before, which is part of what motivated the Red Sox to offer him $130 million over five years last winter. Suarez isn't about to come unglued in Yankee Stadium in two weeks — or any other time he gets the ball in the postseason. His career ERA of 1.48 in the playoffs virtually guarantees that.
"He was very competitive with men on base," said interim manager Chad Tracy. "He lost some counts, was behind more counts today, but he wa able to really good pitches with people on base."
Even as he labored, Suarez was adding to a September resumé which has him 3-0 with 0.92 ERA in his last three outings while limiting opposing hitters to a .186 batting average.
No one knows exactly how or when Suarez will fit into Boston's postseason rotation. The assumption is that Sonny Gray will pitch Game 1, with either Payton Tolle or Suarez slotted for Game 2, and the remaining choice available for a winner-take-all Game 3.
Of course, the risk there is that a team may never get to its third starter if it doesn't win at least one of the first two games. That's part of the difficult decision the Red Sox will have to make before their wild card round gets underway.
Even with his history of success in October, Suarez isn't thinking too much about the postseason — not yet anyway.
"No, no,'' he said with a chuckle. "When we clinch, I'll be able to do that. But mathematically, we're not there yet, so I'm not thinking about that."
Suarez has one more start in the regular season, which he can treat as both a tuneup for himself and an audition for Game 2 in the best-of-three wild card round.,
"He's a very good competitor, a good pitcher that even when he gets traffic, you trust that he's going to find his way through it. He does that at times this year, so that's never a concern with him."

Ranger Suarez (8-4) and three relievers walked nine but held the Rays to five hits. Tampa Bay was hitless in 13 at-bats with runners in scoring position and left 12 men on base.
It was an impressive victory for the Sox, considering the 93-60 Rays are close to clinching the best record in the league and home-field advantage through, at least, the American League Championship Series.
The Sox were without Ceddanne Rafaela, who isn’t expected to come off the injured list until next week. Aroldis Chapman (lat strain) and Willson Contreras (bruised right hand) were not available.
With Garrett Whitlock left in the bullpen after pitching Thursday night, the Sox used lefthander Erik Miller to get the final three outs for his first save with the team.
Miller walked two and threw three wild pitches in a wild ninth inning, giving up a run before finally getting Chandler Simpson to ground to second for the final out.
Miller had allowed five runs over 5⅓ innings and put 10 men on base in his previous six appearances.
The Sox didn’t arrive at the team hotel until close to 5 a.m. after beating the Rangers in Texas on Thursday night. The Rays had a day game at home that ended 13 hours earlier. But the Sox had more energy early on.
Anthony blasted the third pitch of the game from Ian Seymour 438 feet to center field for his fifth home run.
Trevor Story and Caleb Durbin led off the second inning with singles. Isiah Kiner-Falefa dropped a bunt to advance the runners before Nate Eaton worked a walk to load the bases.
After Connor Wong struck out, Anthony worked the count full and lined a hard single to right field to drive in two more runs. The three RBIs matched his career high.
Jahmai Jones homered leading off the third inning, a 414-foot shot to left field.
Suarez did not handle the run support very well. He walked a hitter in each of the first four innings and threw 69 pitches. But the Rays scored only one run.
Yandy Diaz walked leading off the bottom of the first, advanced to third on a double by Jonathan Aranda, and scored on Junior Caminero’s groundout.
Suarez was done after 5⅔ innings and 98 pitches, leaving the game with a runner at second. Wyatt Olds walked Liam Hicks and Victor Mesa Jr. on 12 pitches to load the bases.
He fell behind Jake Fraley 3 and 1, then came back to strike him out swinging through a fastball at the top of the strike zone. Olds threw up his hands after finally ending the inning. It wasn’t an elegant outing, but it was ultimately an effective one.
Greg Weissert worked around a two-out double by Caminero in the seventh inning to keep the lead at three runs, then came back for a 1-2-3 eighth.

Back in late June when the Red Sox sunk to their lowest depths, the idea that the club might still have a shot at reaching the postseason would have seemed hopelessly optimistic.
Yet, here they are with a little over a week left to play in the regular season, and the Red Sox have all but punched their ticket to the playoffs.
With their 4-2 win over the Tampa Bay Rays in Friday’s series opener, the Red Sox can now clinch a playoff spot as soon as Saturday. The club’s magic number, which stood at three entering the night, will drop to either one or two depending on the outcome of Friday’s late game between the Rangers and Blue Jays.
A Rangers win would mean the Red Sox could clinch with a win on Saturday, while a Blue Jays win would necessitate a win and a Blue Jays loss.
Following a string of poor offensive performances, Friday got off to a much stronger start at the plate. Roman Anthony put the Red Sox in front with a solo home run to lead off the game, and after the Rays tied it up in the bottom half of the first, Anthony delivered again in the second with a go-ahead two-run single with the bases loaded off Rays starter Ian Seymour, an alumnus of St. John’s High School in Shrewsbury.
Anthony finished 2 for 4 with three RBI, and the Red Sox never looked back.
“Taking that first one is big,” Anthony told NESN’s Jahmai Webster postgame. “Any win you can get against a team like that it’s a great win, so it’s a great day.”
Anthony’s first-inning blast was smoked. Measured at 107.7 mph off the bat and traveling 438 feet, the solo home run to right field narrowly missed landing in Tropicana Field’s ray tank.
His two-run single in the second inning was hit even harder, coming off the bat at 108.7 mph. Anthony came through after Trevor Story and Caleb Durbin led off the inning with singles, Isiah Kiner-Falefa moved them into scoring position with a sacrifice bunt and Nate Eaton walked to load the bases.
It was doubly encouraging given Anthony’s recent struggles at the plate. After a hot start coming off the injured list, the outfielder came into Friday batting just .137 with one extra base hit over his past 12 games.
“I’ve been grinding, but that’s the beauty of this team,” Anthony said. “You’re never down and you’re never out.”
Jahmai Jones capped off the early offense with a solo shot to lead off the top of the third.
Tampa Bay scored its early run in the first after Yandy Diaz drew a leadoff walk, advanced to third on a Jonathan Aranda double and scored on a Junior Caminero groundout. But that was all the damage the Rays could do against Ranger Suarez, who allowed one run over 5 2/3 innings while falling one out short of his third consecutive quality start.
Suarez was uncharacteristically wild, walking five batters, but he limited the damage by allowing just three hits while striking out five.
The walks almost cost the Red Sox in the sixth inning.
Still leading by three, Suarez issued his fifth and final walk to lead off the sixth before recording two quick outs to finish his outing. But Wyatt Olds came on and immediately walked the first two men he faced, loading the bases and bringing the go-ahead run to the plate.
A brief mound visit followed, and Olds dug deep and struck out pinch hitter Jake Fraley to escape the inning unscathed.
“It was a weird game all the way around, we walked nine in total, Ranger walked five but still almost completed six innings and he was very competitive with men on base,” Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy told reporters in St. Petersburg. “He lost some counts and behind more counts today, but he was able to make really good pitches with people on base.”
Walks put the Red Sox in one more jam in the bottom of the ninth inning.
With Aroldis Chapman unavailable with a lat issue and Garrett Whitlock having pitched on Thursday, Erik Miller took the mound in the ninth and walked three men. He allowed a run to score on a Victor Mesa Jr. groundout, and the third walk to Caminero brought the winning run to the plate with two outs.
Miller struck out Ryan Vilade, but the ball got away from Connor Wong and the Rays batter reached safely to extend the game and load the bases. But Miller fought back and drew a game-ending groundout from Chandler Simpson, leaving the Rays 0 for 13 with runners in scoring position and 12 men left on base in spite of the nine walks issued by the Red Sox pitching staff.
While Miller has now walked seven batters over his last 3 1/3 innings, Tracy said he felt the left-hander looked much better on Friday despite all of the traffic.
“I thought he was way more competitive,” Tracy said. “Everything was around the zone, stuff was good, he was getting some swing and miss like he usually does so I take a lot of good out of that outing.”
The win marked Boston’s first at Tropicana Field this season, and the club hopes plenty more will follow in the days and weeks to come. The Rays have long been in the driver’s seat for the AL East title, and barring a complete collapse over the final week Tampa Bay should soon lock down the American League’s top seed and a bye to the divisional round.
That means if the Red Sox (84-70) can get past the Yankees in the AL Wild Card Series, they’d be headed right back to St. Petersburg to face the Rays in a rematch of the 2021 ALDS.
But first, the Red Sox hope to pop some bottles in the Tropicana Field visitor’s clubhouse before they fly back to Boston. First pitch on Saturday is scheduled for 4:10 p.m.

Red Sox Insert Jahmai Jones into Lineup Against Rays Lefty
The Boston Red Sox placed designated hitter Jahmai Jones in the third spot in the starting lineup on Friday against Tampa Bay Rays left-hander Ian Seymour at Tropicana Field in St. Petersburg, Florida.
According to MLB.com, Jones sits in the heart of the order between outfielders Roman Anthony and Wilyer Abreu. Shortstop Trevor Story and first baseman Nick Sogard also feature in the top five positions for Boston.
Left-hander Ranger Suárez gets the start on the mound for Boston against Tampa Bay's Seymour. Seymour enters the contest holding a 9-6 record with a 4.27 ERA and 150 strikeouts on the season, according to official team statistics.
Boston manager Chad Tracy opted to stack the right-handed hitting Jones near the top of the batting order due to ongoing injuries and lack of availability among several key players, including Ceddanne Rafaela, Masataka Yoshida, Curtis Mead, and Willson Contreras.
According to MLB Trade Rumors, Boston acquired Jones off waivers on July 14 after the Detroit Tigers designated him for assignment, sending pitching prospect Jojo Ingrassia to Detroit as compensation.
Jones struggled with Detroit this season, batting .137 with a .221 slugging percentage across 105 plate appearances before his release. However, he has turned his season around in Boston, slashing .362/.464/.681 with three home runs and eight RBIs in 56 plate appearances.
Friday marks the 20th time overall this season that Jones has occupied the third spot in a starting lineup, having done so 19 times prior across his stints with Detroit and Boston. In those previous 35 plate appearances in the third spot, he posted a .219 batting average and a .661 OPS.
According to FanGraphs, the platoon splits support Boston's heavy usage of Jones against left-handed pitching. Across 138 plate appearances against lefties this year, Jones has recorded a .223 batting average, a .333 on-base percentage, and a .420 slugging percentage with five home runs, 15 walks, and 14 RBIs.
Conversely, Jones has registered just a .130 average in 23 at-bats against right-handed pitchers, with all five of his home runs this season coming exclusively against left-handers. He previously hit a two-run home run off Seymour during a July 18 matchup at Fenway Park.
Boston enters the three-game series against the American League East-leading Rays with an 83-70 record, holding the second AL Wild Card position and a five-game lead over the Cleveland Guardians. NESN reports Boston's magic number to clinch a postseason berth stands at three with nine games remaining on their schedule.

Ahead of the Boston Red Sox series opener at Tropicana Field against the Tampa Bay Rays on Friday, interim manager Chad Tracy met with the media and provided updates on a number of injured Red Sox players.
Here's what you need to know:
All eyes were on the All-Star first baseman after Thursday night's win over the Texas Rangers. Contreras exited the game in the eighth inning after being hit by a pitch on the right-hand. According to MassLive.com's Chris Cotillo, Contreras told reporters after the game that the injury "felt" like a fracture. While initial X-Rays were negative, as the team learned with infielder Curtis Mead, that doesn't mean Contreras was completely out of the woods yet. According to MLB.com's Ian Browne, the team is waiting for swelling in the 34-year-old's hand to subside before testing his grip strength to determine if additional testing is needed.
Contreras is out of the lineup for Friday's series opener.
Crochet threw a 30-pitch up-and-down bullpen session on Tuesday back at Fenway Park, representing the most labor-intensive of the four throwing sessions the 27-year-old has done since restarting a throwing progression Aug. 3. According to WEEI's Rob Bradford, Crochet will throw another side session on Saturday as he continues to work his way back from left shoulder inflammation that has kept him out since April 29.
After turning to Garrett Whitlock to lock down Thursday's win, Tracy told reporters, including Cotillo, that Chapman was unavailable with LAT tightness. According to Bradford, Chapman said the injury popped up ahead of Tuesday's series opener in Texas and that he wasn't concerned about the injury, saying the latest he would return to the mound would be during the team's upcoming home stand, beginning on Tuesday night, if he doesn't make an appearance in Tampa.
Tyron Guerrero
After landing on the injured list on Sept. 1 with right shoulder inflammation. The 35-year-old flamethrower was expected to be activated when he was first eligible, ahead of Wednesday's game in Texas. However, after experiencing lower back tightness, the team delayed his activation. According to Bradford, Guerrero "felt fine" after throwing 20 pitches off the mound on Friday afternoon. However, it still remains unclear when he may be activated.
The 32-year-old outfielder landed on the injured list last Friday with a "right foot ligament injury" after getting it caught in the grates along the center field wall in the Sept. 8 loss to the Los Angeles Angels. As Bradford noted, White has been diagnosed with a ligament tear, likely ending his season.
White's injury seems to open the door for Spring Training standout Braiden Ward to join the Red Sox as a fourth outfielder/pinch runner in the playoffs.
Up next for the Sox
The Red Sox will look to carry the momentum from Thursday's come-from-behind win into the final road series of the year against the Rays. Ranger Suarez (7-4, 3.33 ERA) will get the start for the Red Sox opposite Ian Seymour (9-6, 4.27 ERA) for the Rays. First pitch from Tropicana Field is set for 7:10 p.m. ET.
